title: GPU Fleet: Scaling, Metrics, and On-call Runbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This page documents Redwoodâ€™s operational playbook for the GPU fleet used by Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments. It focuses on three interlinked areas: autoscaling and headroom policy, telemetry and alerting (what to monitor and SLOs), and incident runbooks for common GPU fleet failures. The goal is to give on-call engineers and infra owners a single reference that ties capacity IaC, CI/CD, and day-2 operations together.

Key services and components

- gpu-orchestrator (internal): service that manages rack/node grouping, scaling signals, and quota enforcement. Owned by eng-infra.
- capacity-allocator (internal): decision engine used by scheduler to pick instance families and apply quantization/packing rules.
- tf-mod-gpu-node (Terraform module): standardized module used in cloud accounts to provision GPU node pools.
- ci/gpu-image-build (CI pipeline): produces gpu-runtime images with CUDA/driver versions and small validation suite.
- prometheus/gpu-exporter & grafana (monitoring): fleet metrics ingestion and dashboarding.

SLOs and operational thresholds

- Fleet availability SLO: 99.95% monthly uptime for GPU-serving cluster pools (primary regions). This measures GPU nodes Ready and schedulable across the dedicated pool set.
- Cold-start latency SLO: 95th percentile for first-token latency for cold requests <= 1.5s when using dedicated warm-pools.
- Autoscaler loop target: maintain average GPU utilization per allocation slice between 45â€“65% over rolling 15m.
- Headroom reserve: maintain 10% reserved capacity for burst (configured per pool; 5% for low-priority test pools).

Alerting and paged thresholds (concrete rules)

- Pager (P1) - PoolUnavailable: >= 3 racks in adjacent AZs report node readiness < 85% for 10m. Route to eng-infra on-call.
- Pager (P1) - SchedulerRejects: > 30 scheduling rejects / min sustained for 5m for production pools.
- Pager (P2) - HighGPUUtilization: average GPU utilization > 90% for 10m across >50% nodes in a pool.
- Pager (P2) - DriverOOM: repeated nvidia-driver OOM crashes (driver restarts > 3 times in 15m).
- Pager (P3) - ImageBuildFailure: CI gpu-image-build fails 3 consecutive pipeline runs. Notify infra-dev.

Alert expression examples (PromQL)

- PoolUnavailable: avg by (pool) (kube_node_status_capacity_gpu_count == 0 or kube_node_status_ready == 0) > 0.15 for 10m
- HighGPUUtilization: avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_utilization[10m]) > 90

Note: real PromQL lives in prometheus/alert-rules in our repo.

Autoscaling and headroom policy

Guiding principles

1) Predictability over cost for production pools: prefer slightly over-provisioned nodes to meet latency SLOs.
2) Short-term elasticity for cost-sensitive non-prod pools: aggressive scale-in ok with longer cold-start budgets.
3) Explicit headroom slices: keep reserved capacity (10%) and warm-prewarmed instance groups for cold-start-sensitive workloads.

Autoscaler configuration (recommended defaults)

- Scale up triggers: sustained request queue depth growth > 20% over 5m or observed average GPU util > 65% for 5m.
- Scale down triggers: average GPU util < 40% for 20m and no pending requests.
- Minimum pool size: 4 GPUs (spread across >=2 AZs) for production pools.
- Maximum growth per scaling action: 25% of pool size; cap concurrent scale actions to 2.

Terraform/IaC patterns and modules

- Module names and repo paths: terraform/modules/tf-mod-gpu-node
- Backend: S3-backed state with DynamoDB state locking (aws account per environment).
- Required module variables: region, gpu_instance_type, min_gpus, max_gpus, autoscaler_policy_id, bootstrap_image_tag.

Example module usage (snippet)

```hcl
module "gpu_pool_inference" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra/terraform/modules//tf-mod-gpu-node?ref=v1.8.0"
  region = "us-west-2"
  gpu_instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  min_gpus = 12
  max_gpus = 200
  autoscaler_policy_id = aws_autoscaler_policy.prod_inference.id
  bootstrap_image_tag = "gpu-runtime-2024-11-26"
}
```

- Tagging policy: all GPU nodes must have tags: [env, pool, owner_team, cost_center, gpu_series, cuda_version]. This enables cost allocation and automated upgrades.
- Image upgrades: blue-green at node pool level using ci/gpu-image-build artifacts and tf-mod-gpu-node rolling_update meta-opts. See CI/CD section below.

CI/CD and image build pipeline

Pipeline responsibilities

- Build consistent GPU runtime image with pinned driver, CUDA, cuDNN, and inference-runtime.
- Run smoke validation: containerized inference test across a small model, driver sanity check, and quantization validation.
- Tag artifacts and publish to regional registries.

Pipeline snippet (high level)

1) PR triggers: linting + unit tests
2) Merge to main: nightly builds for stable-major driver; urgent patches trigger hotfix builds.
3) Post-build: run integration suite in ephemeral pool (tf-plan + terraform apply to a dev account pool).

Example GitHub Actions step (abbreviated):

```yaml
- name: Build GPU image
  uses: redwood/actions/gcloud-image-builder@v2
  with:
    image-tag: ${{ inputs.image_tag }}
    cuda-version: 12.1
    driver-version: 535.54

- name: Run smoke tests
  run: ./ci/smoke/gpu-smoke.sh $IMAGE
```

Runbooks: incidents and remediation

P1: PoolUnavailable (multi-rack readiness drop)

1) Pager fires -> immediate acknowledgement.
2) Triage (5m): Check grafana pool dashboard: node readiness, kubelet errors, instance health from cloud console.
3) Check provider status: cloud provider incidents or AZ partial outage. If provider incident, escalate to SRE lead and trigger failover policies (route traffic to secondary region).
4) If not provider outage: examine control-plane logs: gpu-orchestrator, capacity-allocator. Look for failed provisioning API calls or quota errors.
5) Temporary mitigation: increase pool min_gpus by 15% via terraform quick patch (see CLI below) and run tf apply against infra account; OR enable warm-spare pool in secondary AZ.
6) Post-incident: create incident report and a follow-up action item in the capacity backlog.

CLI quick patch example (for emergencies)

```bash
# increase min_gpus in production pool and apply
git checkout -b hotfix/gpu-min-up-$(date +%s)
apply_patch_to_file terraform/prod/gpu_pool.tf \
  'min_gpus = 12' 'min_gpus = 15'
# run plan and apply using automation token
TF_WORKSPACE=prod ./scripts/tf-plan-apply.sh terraform/prod
```

P2: SchedulerRejects (job allocation failures)

1) Acknowledge. Open scheduler logs and filter for "insufficient resources" or "node selector mismatch".
2) Identify whether job requests are malformed (missing nodeAffinity/gpu_type) or if packing rules overconstrain (exclusive vGPU vs shared).
3) If it's malformed requests: roll back the recent deployment or patch the admission webhook that injects node selectors.
4) If capacity-limited: temporarily scale up by adding extra nodes or shifting lower-priority jobs to spot pools.

P2: DriverOOM / Frequent driver restarts

1) Confirm restart pattern: journalctl -u nvidia-driver or driver pod logs.
2) If a specific kernel/driver combo causes OOMs, pin new instances to a safe driver version and schedule gradual replacement.
3) As stopgap: cordon affected nodes and trigger rolling replacement; notify model teams to reduce batch size if possible.

Capacity planning and forecasting

- Monthly cadence: capacity review every 1st Wednesday. Inputs: growth forecasts (product), recent token-per-second trends, large upcoming customers, and new model rollouts.
- 90-day runway target: maintain 20% spare capacity buffer above expected growth from committed customers.
- Forecasting data sources: request-rate time series from api-gateway, token consumption from billing tables, cluster utilization from prometheus.

Ownership and escalation matrix

- Primary on-call: eng-infra on-call rotation (contact: #eng-infra-oncall).
- Secondary: eng-sre on-call.
- Escalation to PagerDuty level 2 (SRE lead) if incident > 30m or customer-impacting outage.
- Customer communication: CS/Support should be looped in for incidents > 15m affecting SLA customers.

Maintenance windows and planned work

- Weekly maintenance window: Tuesdays 02:00â€“05:00 UTC for routine node kernel/driver upgrades in non-prod.
- Production upgrades: scheduled quarterly with canary pools (5â€“10% of nodes), announce 72h in advance to affected customers.

Post-incident follow-up checklist

1) Add root-cause analysis to Wiki within 48h.
2) Implement at least one corrective action within 2 weeks (automation, test, or config guard).
3) Validate mitigation by running targeted chaos tests (simulated AZ failure, driver crash).
4) Update terraform module defaults if needed.

Appendix: useful commands and links

- Grafana: https://grafana.internal.redwood.ai/d/gpu-fleet
- Prometheus rules repo: git@repo.redwood.ai:infra/observability/alert-rules.git
- Terraform module: git@repo.redwood.ai:infra/terraform/modules/tf-mod-gpu-node.git
- CI pipeline: https://ci.internal.redwood.ai/pipelines/gpu-image-build

Common commands

- Check node GPU readiness: kubectl get nodes -l pool=prod-gpu -o wide
- Cordon and drain node: kubectl cordon $NODE && kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Trigger a small scale-up: ./scripts/scale-pool.sh --pool prod-gpu --increase 3

Contact list

- eng-infra rotation: #eng-infra-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Capacity product liaison: Priya Desai (priya@redwood.ai)
- SRE lead: Ethan Brooks (ethan@redwood.ai)

This document is the authoritative on-call and operational reference for the GPU fleet. For related IaC patterns, see the terraform modules and CI/CD build docs linked above.
